P01.note: Plural head 'rent ceilings' plus past tense from 'voted' in the unless-clause. 'have been provisional' is the strongest distractor because the passage opens in the present.
P01.not_hard_because: The head noun 'ceilings' and the intervening 'blocks' are both plural, so there is no attractor and number is free; only the tense needs 'voted'.

P02.note: Plural 'goats' takes 'devour'; 'it' refers to the singular plant, giant hogweed. 'devours' is pulled by the singular 'dairy' right before the blank; 'them' by 'blisters'.
P02.not_hard_because: Same verb-plus-pronoun grid as nine other items, where the key always pairs a verb and pronoun of opposite number; 'the plant' later in the sentence confirms the singular antecedent.

P03.note: Elliptical clause parallel to 'was salvageable': plural 'ceilings' needs 'were not [salvageable]'. 'have not' tempts as a present-perfect negative but cannot elide 'salvageable'.
P03.not_hard_because: The parallel clause 'The proscenium was salvageable' hands over the verb 'be' and the past tense, leaving only number, and 'ceilings' is a plain plural.

P04.note: Elliptical 'does not [discharge water at a constant rate]' copies present-tense 'discharge' in the main clause; singular 'geyser'. 'was not' tempts because the later sentences shift to past.
P04.not_hard_because: The main clause verb 'discharge' gives away both the auxiliary 'do' and the present tense; the same ellipsis template recurs in P03, P13 and P26.

P05.note: Singular 'drill' with present 'decide' in the while-clause gives 'is being run'. 'are being run' is pulled by 'layers' just before the blank.
P05.not_hard_because: The tense is handed over by 'decide' in the while-clause and the distractor is the standard attractor noun ('layers') directly before the blank, the same build as P10, P18 and P23.

P06.note: Singular 'archive' takes 'has'; 'them' refers back to the plural 'registers' that were divided and reunited. 'have' is pulled by 'towns'.
P06.not_hard_because: Key mixes singular verb with plural pronoun exactly as in every other verb-plus-pronoun grid in this render; the 'divided ... reunited' pairing makes 'registers' the obvious antecedent.

P07.note: 'Cattle' is an invariably plural noun, and 'provided that the animals drink' sets present tense, giving 'are safe'. 'is safe' tempts students who treat 'cattle' as a mass noun.
P07.not_hard_because: The word 'farms' just before the blank is plural and 'the animals' later restates plural, so the attractor pushes toward the key rather than away.

P08.convention: Singular possessive 'copyist's' is grammatical; only the context of two copyists decides number, and a reader could take one surviving hand as meant
P08.note: Two copyists prepared the parts, so their joint work is 'copyists''. The single handwriting description (one clef slant, one stem habit) makes 'copyist's' attractive and arguably defensible.
P08.not_hard_because: Number is decided by 'Two copyists' in the first sentence, a context read rather than a structural one; B and D lack the apostrophe a possessive before 'work' needs.

P09.note: Samples were drawn in all four barns, so 'drawn in the barn nearest the duck pond' is restrictive and takes no punctuation. A comma or dash would make it nonrestrictive, implying every sample came from that barn; the dash is the strongest distractor because a lone sentence-final dash is legal in form.

P10.note: Compound subject 'The fresco and the gilded screen' is plural; 'each winter unless ... installs' is present habitual, giving 'are darkening'. 'is darkening' is pulled by 'chancel'.
P10.not_hard_because: 'and' in the subject makes the plural obvious and 'installs' hands over present tense; the singular attractor 'chancel' is the same trap as P05, P18, P23.

P11.note: Plural 'Applications', past tense from 'arrived' and 'had withdrawn' in the if-clause, so 'were routed'. 'have been routed' tempts because the first sentence uses 'has been held up'.
P11.not_hard_because: Same template as P01: plural head, singular attractor ('employer'), tense given by the past verb in the following conditional clause; the present-perfect options never win in this render.

P12.convention: 'its' can be read as the office's repayments (the repayments it handled), with the office as the nearest singular antecedent
P12.note: Singular 'office' takes 'was copying'; the repayments belong to the borrowers, so 'their' is the natural pronoun. 'its' is defensible if read as the repayments the office received, so the pronoun half is ambiguous.
P12.not_hard_because: Number of the verb is plain from 'the branch office'; the only difficulty is a pronoun whose antecedent is genuinely ambiguous, which is a defect, not difficulty. The opposite-number pairing tell also picks D.

P13.note: Elliptical 'have not [withstood ...]' copies present-perfect 'has withstood'; plural 'cultivars'. 'do not' tempts as a present negative.
P13.not_hard_because: 'has withstood' in the main clause hands over the auxiliary 'have' and only number remains, with 'cultivars' plainly plural; same ellipsis template as P03, P04, P26.

P14.note: Singular 'rash' with present perfect 'has ... reappeared'; the appositive 'blisters' pulls toward 'have'. 'is/are ... reappeared' is never grammatical.
P14.not_hard_because: 'reappeared' after the blank rules out both 'is' and 'are' at a glance, leaving a binary has/have choice with the head noun 'rash' named in the subject.

P15.note: Plural 'gospel books' takes 'were'; 'its' refers to the abbey (Reichenau). 'their' has no sensible plural antecedent other than the books themselves, which would be circular.
P15.not_hard_because: The plural subject sits immediately before the blank with no intervening attractor, and the verb-plus-pronoun grid again keys on opposite numbers.

P16.note: Plural 'cables', with 'on the morning of the volcano's largest explosion' fixing a past moment, gives 'were carrying'. 'has been carrying' is pulled by 'station'.
P16.not_hard_because: A specific past time phrase after the blank hands over the tense and the singular 'station' attractor is the same trap as most items here; the present-perfect options never win.

P17.note: Singular 'crypt' takes 'was bypassed'; 'them' refers to the pilgrims. 'were' is pulled by 'transepts'; 'by it' has no sensible singular agent.
P17.not_hard_because: 'by it' produces an absurd agent (the shrine or crypt bypassing itself), so the pronoun half is nearly free, and the verb grid matches the opposite-number pattern.

P18.note: Singular 'census' with present 'detects' in the if-clause gives 'is updated'. 'are updated' is pulled by 'asteroids'.
P18.not_hard_because: 'detects' hands over present tense and 'asteroids' is the standard plural attractor between head and blank, same build as P05, P10, P23.

P19.note: Singular 'trial'; 'during the first rainy season of the project' is a completed past period, so 'was suspended'. 'has been suspended' is the strongest distractor since the report is described in the present.
P19.not_hard_because: A finished past time phrase follows the blank and the plural attractor 'vaccines' is the usual trap; present-perfect options lose in every tense grid here.

P20.note: Plural 'crews' takes 'were covering'; 'it' is the dish. 'them' is pulled by 'wind farms', which also make the plural verb feel right.
P20.not_hard_because: The plural subject is unmistakable and the opening 'To protect ... lone radio dish' names the singular antecedent; opposite-number pairing again.

P21.note: Singular 'archivist' takes 'is digitizing'; 'them' is the six hundred recordings. 'it' has no fitting singular antecedent.
P21.not_hard_because: 'sole archivist' is emphatically singular and 'one cassette at a time' points to many recordings; opposite-number pairing again.

P22.note: Singular 'portrait', with 'during the first half of the eighteenth century' fixing a completed past, gives 'was obscure'. 'were obscure' is pulled by 'sisters'.
P22.not_hard_because: A completed past period after the blank hands over the tense and the plural attractor 'sisters' is the same trap as P16, P19, P28.

P23.note: Singular 'rivalry' with present 'announce' and 'each September' gives 'is chronicled'. 'are chronicled' is pulled by 'bands'.
P23.not_hard_because: 'announce ... each September' hands over present habitual tense and 'bands' is the usual attractor; same build as P05, P10, P18.

P24.note: Plural 'teams' takes 'are tracking'; the plumes belong to the only active vent ('its'), not the older volcanoes, which the passage implies are inactive. 'their' is attractive because 'volcanoes' is the nearest plural noun.
P24.not_hard_because: The verb half is free from 'survey teams', and the pronoun is settled once a reader notices 'only active vent'; opposite-number pairing also picks it.

P25.note: 'Each graft and cutting' takes a singular verb despite the compound, and 'before the growers recognized' sets past, giving 'was developing'. 'were developing' is attractive from the compound subject and the plural 'trays'.

P26.note: Elliptical 'are not [eligible]' parallels 'are eligible'; 'the unemployed' (adjective as noun) is plural. 'is not' tempts students who read 'the unemployed' as singular.
P26.not_hard_because: The parallel clause 'are eligible' hands over the exact verb, and the plural 'districts' right before the blank pushes toward the key; same ellipsis template as P03, P04, P13.

P27.note: The inverted 'should the first reading lessons be taught' is a direct question, so it ends with a question mark and 'Their' starts a new sentence. A is a comma splice, C a fused sentence, D treats a direct question as a statement.
P27.not_hard_because: The inversion 'should the ... lessons be' signals a direct question at once, and two of the three distractors are routine sentence-boundary errors.

P28.note: Singular 'hum' with past 'peaked' gives 'was audible'. 'were audible' is pulled by 'fans' directly before the blank.
P28.not_hard_because: 'peaked' hands over past tense and 'fans' is the standard attractor; the same subject-of-prepositional-chain build as P16, P19, P22.

P29.note: Singular 'camera' takes 'records'; 'their' refers to the infants. 'record' is pulled by 'puppets' in the previous clause; 'its' has no sensible antecedent (the stage's reactions).
P29.not_hard_because: The subject 'a camera' is plainly singular and 'its reactions' is absurd; opposite-number pairing again.

P30.note: Plural 'volunteers' takes 'have relined'; 'its' refers to the pond. 'has' is pulled by 'office'.
P30.not_hard_because: The because-clause names the singular pond up front and 'their banks' (volunteers' banks) is absurd; opposite-number pairing again.

P31.note: Two independent clauses ('left a circular opening' / 'a ring ... refroze'); the semicolon joins them. The colon is the strongest distractor, but the second clause reports a later event rather than explaining the opening; A is a comma splice, D a fused sentence.
P31.not_hard_because: The long subject 'a ring of shattered ice blocks around its rim' is the only obstacle; once the second verb 'refroze' is found it is a standard semicolon-versus-splice item.

P32.note: Singular possessive: the plans belong to the single mayor named in the first sentence. 'mayors'' is the only real distractor.
P32.not_hard_because: 'a single mayor' in the first sentence hands over the number, and 'mayors' without an apostrophe before a noun is never right; same possessive template as P08.

tells: In every verb-plus-pronoun 2x2 grid (P02, P06, P12, P15, P17, P20, P21, P24, P29, P30) the key pairs a verb and a pronoun of OPPOSITE number (singular verb + plural pronoun or plural verb + singular pronoun). A test-taker who solves only the verb can take the pronoun of the other number without reading for the antecedent.
In every tense-plus-number grid, the present-perfect options ('has/have been ...') never win: P01, P11, P16, P19, P22 all offer them and all key on a simple or progressive form.

Agreement items nearly always place a noun of the WRONG number directly before the blank (P05 layers, P10 chancel, P11 employer, P14 blisters, P16 station, P18 asteroids, P19 vaccines, P22 sisters, P23 bands, P25 trays, P28 fans); 'choose the verb that disagrees with the noun next to the blank' gets these right. Exceptions where the adjacent noun agrees (P01, P07, P26) are the few where the trap is absent.
Tense is always handed over by an explicit later clause or time phrase (unless/if/while/before clause or 'on the morning of'), so tense never requires inference across sentences.
Ellipsis items (P03, P04, P13, P26) always key on the auxiliary that copies the first clause's verb form.
Keys are evenly distributed (8 each of A-D on my answers), so no letter tell.
